checks.title: Global Administrator count between two and five
remediation: Reduce permanent Global Administrators to the break-glass accounts plus at most a few named people.
Move day-to-day administration to least-privilege roles and make the remaining Global Administrator assignments eligible in PIM with approval and a time limit.

userImpact.text: Administrators who lose standing Global Administrator activate it in PIM when they need it, a minute or two each time.

checks.narrative: Every Global Administrator is a full tenant takeover away from any phishing kit or malware on that person's machine. Microsoft recommends fewer than five, and two is the floor because the break-glass accounts hold the role. Counts above that usually come from convenience assignments that nobody revisited.

checks.title: No permanent privileged assignments outside break-glass
remediation: Convert each permanent privileged assignment listed to a PIM eligible assignment with activation MFA, justification, a maximum duration of eight hours or less, and approval for Global Administrator.
Keep only the break-glass accounts permanent.

userImpact.text: Administrators activate their role in PIM before admin work, with MFA and a reason; everyone else sees nothing.

checks.narrative: A standing privileged role is a standing target. Eligible assignments mean the role exists only for the hours it is activated, every activation is logged with a reason, and an attacker who lands in the account outside that window gets a normal user. This is what Entra ID P2 is for.

checks.title: No administrators synced from on-premises AD
remediation: Create cloud-only accounts for the administrators listed.
Assign the roles to those accounts.
Remove the roles from the synced accounts. Cloud-only admin accounts do not inherit an on-premises compromise.

userImpact.text: Administrators sign in to a separate cloud-only account for admin work.

checks.narrative: A synced account's password and status are controlled from on-premises Active Directory. If a domain controller falls, every synced administrator falls with it, and the attacker reaches the cloud without touching it. Microsoft's guidance for protecting Microsoft 365 from on-premises attacks starts with cloud-only privileged accounts.

checks.title: Administrator accounts are unlicensed, separate identities
remediation: Give each administrator a separate admin account with no mailbox and no Microsoft 365 license, used only for administration.
Remove the roles from the daily-use licensed account.

userImpact.text: Administrators keep two accounts: the daily one for mail and Teams, the admin one for the portals.

checks.narrative: An administrator who reads mail and browses with the same account exposes the role to every phishing message and drive-by download. A separate, unlicensed admin account has no mailbox to phish and no Office session to hijack. Licenses on it are the tell that it doubles as a daily account.

checks.title: Break-glass accounts exist, are cloud-only and enabled
remediation: Create two cloud-only emergency access accounts with long random passwords stored offline.
Assign them Global Administrator permanently.
Exclude them from every Conditional Access policy that blocks (CA-012).
Alert on any sign-in by either account.
Name them in the profile so the checks recognise them.

userImpact.text: Nobody sees these accounts; they sit unused until an emergency.

checks.narrative: When MFA, federation or a policy misfire locks every administrator out, the break-glass accounts are the only way back in. They must be cloud-only so an on-premises outage cannot take them, enabled so they work, and excluded from blocking policies so the lockout does not apply to them.

checks.title: PIM activation settings on the top roles
checks.remediation: In PIM, for Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Security Administrator and Conditional Access Administrator: require MFA on activation, require justification, cap activation at eight hours, and require approval for Global Administrator.

userImpact.text: Administrators answer MFA and give a reason when they activate a role; Global Administrator waits for an approver.

checks.narrative: Eligible assignments only help if activation is harder than a click. MFA on activation stops a stolen session from elevating, a duration cap limits how long an activated role lives, and approval on Global Administrator puts a second person between an attacker and the tenant.

checks.title: No service principal holds Global Administrator
remediation: Replace Global Administrator on any service principal with the specific Graph application permissions or the narrowest directory role the workload needs.
Review every service principal listed and record the owner and purpose of each role it keeps.

userImpact.text: No people involved; the app owner may need to re-grant narrower permissions to the workload.

checks.narrative: A service principal with a directory role is an administrator with no MFA, no sign-in frequency and usually a secret somewhere in a pipeline. Global Administrator on one of them is the most direct path from a leaked secret to full tenant control.

checks.title: User consent limited to admin consent or verified low-impact apps
remediation: In Enterprise applications, consent and permissions, set user consent to Do not allow, or to Allow for verified publishers for selected permissions only.
Enable the admin consent workflow (ID-009) so users have a path to request access.

userImpact.text: Users can no longer consent to new apps themselves; they request access and wait for an admin to approve.

checks.narrative: Consent phishing asks a user to approve an app that reads their mail and files. If users can consent to any permission, one click gives the attacker a persistent OAuth grant that survives password changes and MFA. Restricting consent closes the door; the workflow keeps legitimate requests moving.

checks.title: Admin consent workflow enabled with reviewers
remediation: Enable the admin consent request workflow and name at least two reviewers who hold a role able to grant consent.
Set request expiry and reviewer notifications.

userImpact.text: Users who hit a consent prompt get a request button instead of a dead end.

checks.narrative: Once user consent is restricted, users need a way to ask. Without the workflow they ask by email or not at all, and administrators grant tenant-wide consent to get them unblocked, which is worse than the user consent that was removed.

checks.title: No expired or soon-to-expire application credentials
remediation: For each app listed, remove expired secrets and certificates, rotate the ones expiring soon, and record an owner.
Prefer certificates or federated credentials over secrets, and alert on expiry from the registration owner's calendar or a monitoring job.

userImpact.text: No user change if credentials are rotated before they expire; an expired one already breaks the app.

checks.narrative: An expired credential on a live integration is an outage waiting for the next token refresh. Expired credentials left in place also hide which ones are actually in use. Thirty days is the window in which rotation can be scheduled rather than done in an incident.

checks.title: High-privilege application permissions justified
remediation: For each grant listed, confirm the workload still exists and needs that permission.
Replace tenant-wide permissions with resource-specific consent or a narrower permission, and remove the rest.
Record the surviving grants as exceptions with an owner and a review date.

userImpact.text: An app whose permission is narrowed may lose a feature nobody was using; check with its owner first.

checks.narrative: An application permission applies to every mailbox, site or user in the tenant with no user present. Directory.ReadWrite.All or Mail.ReadWrite on a forgotten app is a complete data exfiltration path that bypasses Conditional Access entirely. Each one should have a name next to it.

checks.title: No guests inactive beyond the threshold
remediation: Remove or disable the guests listed.
Put an access review on guest access so inactive guests are removed on a schedule rather than by hand. Entra ID Governance can automate the removal.

userImpact.text: Removed guests lose access; active guests are not affected.

checks.narrative: A guest who has not signed in for months still holds whatever was shared with them, under an identity another organisation controls. Inactive guests are the longest-lived access in most tenants and the least looked at.

checks.title: Cross-tenant inbound access reviewed, not default-open
remediation: Review the inbound B2B collaboration defaults: restrict which external users and groups can be invited and to which applications, decide whether to trust external MFA and device claims, and add per-partner settings for the organisations you work with.
Record the decision as an exception if the open default is intentional.

userImpact.text: Partner users outside the allowed organisations can no longer be invited; existing guests are not affected.

checks.narrative: The default cross-tenant settings allow any external user to be invited to any application. That is fine for an organisation that has decided it, and a gap for one that never looked. The check fails on the untouched default so the decision gets made.

checks.title: Sign-in and audit logs exported to Log Analytics or a SIEM
checks.remediation: Add a diagnostic setting on Entra ID that sends SignInLogs, AuditLogs, NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs and RiskyUsers to a Log Analytics workspace or your SIEM, with retention beyond the 30 days the portal keeps.

userImpact.text: An admin setting users never see.

checks.narrative: Entra keeps sign-in logs for seven to thirty days depending on license. An incident discovered later than that has no evidence to investigate. Exporting the logs is a one-time setting and the difference between knowing what happened and guessing.

checks.title: No high-risk users left unaddressed
remediation: Investigate each user listed in Identity Protection: confirm the compromise or dismiss the risk.
For a confirmed compromise, reset the password and revoke the user's sessions.
Enable the user-risk policy (CA-004) so future high-risk users are remediated automatically.

userImpact.text: The users listed reset their password and sign in again.

checks.narrative: A user flagged high risk has leaked credentials or attacker-pattern sign-ins. A week without action means either nobody is watching the report or the user-risk policy is missing. Either way the account is still usable by whoever triggered the detection.

checks.title: No sign-ins over legacy protocols in the sign-in log
remediation: Move each account listed to modern authentication: Outlook or a current mail client instead of IMAP and POP, OAuth for SMTP AUTH senders such as scanners and line-of-business apps.
Then block legacy authentication with Conditional Access. The list is who would stop working when the block goes on.

userImpact.text: Anyone still on IMAP, POP or basic SMTP AUTH stops connecting until their app or device moves to modern sign-in.

checks.narrative: Legacy protocols send a password with every request and cannot ask for MFA, so a guessed or leaked password is enough. Password spraying aims at them for that reason. The sign-in log shows who still depends on them, which is the list to fix before blocking.

checks.title: Cloud passwords do not expire on a schedule
remediation: In the Microsoft 365 admin center, Settings, Org settings, Security and privacy, Password expiration policy, set passwords to never expire.
Keep MFA and the banned password list doing the work periodic changes used to do; force a change only when a password is known or suspected to be compromised.

userImpact.text: People stop being made to change their password every few months.

checks.narrative: NIST SP 800-63B and Microsoft both advise against periodic password changes: people respond with predictable variations (Spring2026!, Summer2026!) that attackers guess first. Expiry adds help desk calls and no protection once MFA is in place; a change belongs after a suspected compromise.

checks.title: Custom banned password list in use
remediation: In Entra, Authentication methods, Password protection, set Enforce custom list to Yes.
Add the words people reach for here: the organisation's name and abbreviations, products, sports teams and the city. Up to 1,000 terms; Microsoft also blocks variations and its own global list.

userImpact.text: People choosing a new password that contains a blocked word are asked to pick another.

checks.narrative: NIST SP 800-63B asks for new passwords to be checked against words likely to be guessed. Microsoft's global list covers common passwords; only the custom list knows the organisation's own name, products and places, which are the first words a password spray tries.

checks.title: Password protection enforced on-premises
remediation: Install the Entra Password Protection proxy service and the domain controller agent on every domain controller, then check in the Entra admin center that each agent reports in.
In Entra, Password protection, set Enable password protection on Windows Server Active Directory to Yes and the mode to Enforced, after a period in Audit.

userImpact.text: People changing an on-premises password to a banned word are asked to pick another, the same as in the cloud.

checks.narrative: With synced identities the password is set in Active Directory, so the cloud banned list only protects what changes in the cloud. The agents carry the same list to the domain controllers; in Audit mode they only log.

checks.title: Guests cannot invite other guests
remediation: In Entra, External Identities, External collaboration settings, set Guest invite settings to Only users assigned to specific admin roles can invite guest users, or Member users and users assigned to specific admin roles.
Give the Guest Inviter role to the people who bring in partners, if members should not invite freely.

userImpact.text: Guests can no longer invite other guests; members and guest inviters invite as before.

checks.narrative: When guests can invite guests, one compromised or careless partner account can bring in anyone, and nobody in the organisation approved them. Keeping invitations with members or named inviters keeps a person accountable for every guest.

checks.title: Guest access limited to their own objects
remediation: In Entra, External Identities, External collaboration settings, set Guest user access to Guest user access is restricted to properties and memberships of their own directory objects (most restrictive), or at least limited access.

userImpact.text: Guests keep working in the teams and sites they were invited to; they just cannot browse the directory.

checks.narrative: A guest with the same directory access as members can list every user, group and device, which is reconnaissance for phishing and a map of the organisation. Restricted access is CISA's baseline and breaks nothing guests normally do.

checks.title: Outbound guest access to other tenants reviewed
remediation: In Entra, External Identities, Cross-tenant access settings, Default settings, review Outbound access settings for B2B collaboration.
Block the default and allow the partner organisations people work with under Organizational settings, or limit the default to a group.
If the open default is intended, record it as an accepted risk with the reason.

userImpact.text: People can accept guest invitations only from the partner organisations allowed; others are refused at sign-in.

checks.narrative: By default every user can accept a guest invitation to any other Microsoft 365 tenant and take the organisation's files into it under their work identity. Allowing only known partners closes a quiet exfiltration route that data loss prevention does not watch.

checks.title: Admin command-line tools open only to the people who need them
remediation: For each tool listed, open its enterprise application (create it first with New-MgServicePrincipal -AppId <id> if the tenant has none yet), set Assignment required to Yes, and assign a group of the administrators and developers who use it, including the account that runs TenantKeep Posture.
Or block the tools in Conditional Access for everyone except that group; for Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, blocking Windows Azure Service Management for everyone else does the same.
Note that Restrict access to Microsoft Entra admin center only hides the portal: it does not stop PowerShell or Graph.

userImpact.text: Only people outside the assigned group notice: Graph PowerShell, the Azure CLI and the other shells refuse their sign-in. Most users never run them.

checks.narrative: Any member can sign in to Graph PowerShell, Graph Explorer, the Azure CLI or the Exchange, SharePoint and Teams shells and read whatever their account can see: the whole directory, groups, devices and much of the configuration. Attackers with a stolen password or token use exactly these tools, because they are trusted Microsoft apps with consent already in place. Limiting them to the people who need them removes a ready-made reconnaissance kit from every ordinary account.

checks.title: No application holds Graph permissions it has stopped using
remediation: For each application listed, find its owner and ask whether it is still in use.
Remove the application permissions of one that is not, or delete its enterprise application and app registration.
For one that runs rarely (a yearly job), record it as an exception with its owner and when it next runs.

userImpact.text: None for an application nobody uses. One that runs once a year stops the next time it runs if its permissions were removed, so ask first.

checks.narrative: An application permission works with no user present, for as long as the application has a credential. An application that has not signed in for months and still holds permissions on Microsoft Graph is access nobody is watching: its secret can be in an old script, a retired server or a former supplier's hands. Applications made in the last 90 days are too new to judge and are left out.

checks.title: Only administrators can register applications
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Identity, Users, User settings.
Set "Users can register applications" to No.
Give the Application Developer role to the people who do need to register apps.

userImpact.text: Someone who tries to register an app is told to ask an administrator. Apps that exist keep working.

checks.narrative: Any user who can register an app can create one with a secret, give it a convincing name and ask colleagues to consent to it. Forgotten test apps with credentials start the same way. Limiting registration to a role keeps the list of apps to ones somebody answers for.

checks.title: Handing out a privileged role alerts someone
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Identity Governance, Privileged Identity Management, Microsoft Entra roles, Roles.
For each listed role open Role settings, Edit, Notifications.
Under the two role assignment alerts (members assigned as eligible, members assigned as active), keep the default recipients on or add the mailbox your security team reads.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. Administrators get an email when a privileged role is given to someone.

checks.narrative: An attacker who reaches one administrator account gives a second account a role so the access survives a password reset. The alert on a new assignment is how that is noticed the same day. Role by role, the alert can be switched off, and then a new Global Administrator appears without a word.

checks.title: Activating a privileged role alerts someone
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Identity Governance, Privileged Identity Management, Microsoft Entra roles, Roles.
For each listed role open Role settings, Edit, Notifications.
Under the role activation alert (eligible members activate this role), keep the default recipients on or add the mailbox your security team reads.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. Administrators get an email when someone activates a privileged role.

checks.narrative: Just-in-time roles only help if somebody sees the activations. An activation of Global Administrator at three in the morning from an account that never does that is the clearest signal PIM gives, and it is an email nobody receives when the alert has no recipient.

checks.title: New client secrets are refused on applications
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Security, Application policies.
Open Block password addition, set it to On for all applications, and leave the date empty so older applications are covered too.
Move the applications that still use a secret to a certificate or a federated credential first, or give the few that cannot move an exception policy of their own.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. A developer who tries to add a client secret is refused and uses a certificate or a federated credential.

checks.narrative: A client secret is a password for an application: it sits in a configuration file, a pipeline variable or a script, and it works from anywhere with no MFA. An attacker with rights over an application adds a secret of their own and keeps the access after the person they phished changes a password. Refusing new secrets closes both.

checks.title: Application secrets and certificates have a maximum lifetime
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Security, Application policies.
Open Restrict max password lifetime and Restrict max certificate lifetime, set each to On for all applications, with about half a year for secrets and a year for certificates.
Leave the date empty so the limit covers older applications when their credentials are next renewed.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. Whoever looks after an application renews its secret or certificate on a schedule.

checks.narrative: The portal offers two years for a secret and lets a script ask for a hundred. A credential nobody has to renew is one nobody remembers, and it keeps working long after the person who made it has left. A maximum lifetime turns every credential into something that is looked at again.

checks.title: Only administrators can create tenants
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Users, User settings.
Set Restrict non-admin users from creating tenants to Yes.
Give the Tenant Creator role to the few people who do need to create one.

userImpact.text: Someone who needs a new tenant asks a person who holds the Tenant Creator role.

checks.narrative: Anyone in the directory can create a new Entra tenant and is its Global Administrator from the first minute. That tenant is outside your policies, your logs and your offboarding, and it is a quiet place to move company data to or to run an app registration from.

checks.title: Only administrators can create security groups
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Users, User settings.
Set Users can create security groups to No.
If teams should still manage their own membership, make them owners of groups an administrator creates.

userImpact.text: People ask for a security group instead of creating one. Owners still manage the members of their groups.

checks.narrative: Security groups are what access is granted to: applications, SharePoint sites, licences, exclusions from a policy. A group anyone can create, with any name, is one that ends up in a permission list because it sounded official.

checks.title: Creating Microsoft 365 groups is limited to the people you choose
remediation: Decide who may create a team, a group mailbox or a Planner plan, and put them in one security group.

The admin center has no switch for this. With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, set EnableGroupCreation to false and GroupCreationAllowedGroupId to that group in the Group.Unified directory setting (Microsoft's page below has the script).
Tell everyone else how to ask for one.

userImpact.text: People outside the chosen group can no longer create a team, a Microsoft 365 group or a plan, and ask for one instead.

checks.narrative: Every Microsoft 365 group brings a mailbox, a SharePoint site and often a team, each with its own sharing. When everyone can create them, the tenant fills with groups nobody owns and sites nobody reviews, which is where overshared files and forgotten guests live.

checks.title: Nobody gets an account with an email address alone
remediation: Neither setting has a switch in the admin center.
With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, as a Global Administrator: Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -AllowedToSignUpEmailBasedSubscriptions:$false -AllowEmailVerifiedUsersToJoinOrganization:$false
Read the authorization policy back (Get-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy) and check both values are False.

userImpact.text: Someone who signs up for a Microsoft trial with a work address is told to ask an administrator.

checks.narrative: With these two settings on, anyone who can receive mail at one of your domains can create themselves an account in your directory, by signing up for a self-service product or by proving they own the address. A shared mailbox, a forgotten alias or a contractor's forwarded address is enough, and the account never went through onboarding.

checks.title: Administrators cannot reset their own password by self-service
remediation: The admin center has no switch for this.
With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, as a Global Administrator: Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -AllowedToUseSspr:$false
Make sure at least two administrators can reset each other's passwords, and that the break-glass accounts are tested.

userImpact.text: An administrator who forgets a password asks another administrator to reset it.

checks.narrative: Self-service reset for an administrator is a second way into the most powerful accounts in the tenant, and it is guarded by a phone number and a mailbox, not by the sign-in rules you wrote for administrators. Sending those resets through another administrator puts a person in the path.

checks.title: Risky consent requests go to an administrator
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Consent and permissions, User consent settings, and check what users may consent to.
Risk-based step-up consent is on unless someone turned it off. To turn it back on with Microsoft Graph PowerShell: Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -AllowUserConsentForRiskyApps:$false
If the tenant has a consent settings object, set BlockUserConsentForRiskyApps to true there as well.

userImpact.text: A person who is asked to approve an app Microsoft judges risky sees that an administrator has to approve it.

checks.narrative: Consent phishing sends a real Microsoft consent screen for the attacker's app. Microsoft marks a request as risky when the publisher is unverified and the app asks for more than the basics, and by default sends it to an administrator. With that switched off, the person the attacker picked is the only reviewer.

checks.title: Group owners cannot consent to apps for their groups
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Consent and permissions, User consent settings.
Under Group owner consent for apps accessing data, choose Do not allow group owner consent.
Send owners who need an app in their team to the admin consent workflow.

userImpact.text: A team owner who wants an app that reads the team's data asks an administrator.

checks.narrative: An owner of a team can let an app read that team's messages and files without anyone else seeing the request. Owners are picked for running a project, not for judging what an app will do with a year of conversation.

checks.title: Admin consent requests reach a reviewer and expire
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Consent and permissions, Admin consent settings.
Turn on the email notification for new requests and the reminder before a request expires.
Set the request to expire after 30 days or fewer.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. Reviewers get an email when someone asks for an app.

checks.narrative: The workflow replaces a person approving an app on their own with a request to a reviewer. If the reviewer is never told, the request sits until it lapses, and the person who asked finds another way to get the app.

checks.title: Smart lockout stops password guessing within ten tries
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Protection, Authentication methods, Password protection.
Set Lockout threshold to 10 or lower and Lockout duration in seconds to 60 or higher.
Changing these needs Entra ID P1; Microsoft's defaults already meet the check.

userImpact.text: Someone who mistypes a password many times waits a minute before trying again.

checks.narrative: Smart lockout is what makes guessing a password slow: after so many wrong tries from an unfamiliar place the account refuses further guesses for a while. A threshold raised to stop help desk calls, or a lockout shortened to seconds, gives an attacker thousands of guesses a day at every account.

checks.title: Guests cannot own Microsoft 365 groups
remediation: The admin center has no switch for this.
With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, set AllowGuestsToBeGroupOwner to false in the Group.Unified directory setting (Microsoft's page below shows how to read and change these settings).
List the groups a guest owns today and give each an owner from your own organisation.

userImpact.text: A guest can be a member of a group or a team and can no longer be made its owner.

checks.narrative: The owner of a group decides who is in it, and with it who reads its mailbox, its site and its team. A guest as owner means somebody outside the organisation is adding and removing people from your data, under their own employer's security, not yours.

checks.title: The MSOnline PowerShell module is blocked
remediation: The admin center has no switch for this.
With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, as a Global Administrator: Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -BlockMsolPowerShell:$true
Move any script that still loads MSOnline to Microsoft Graph PowerShell first; Microsoft has retired the module.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for users. A script that still uses the MSOnline module stops working.

checks.narrative: MSOnline is the oldest way to script the directory, and any signed-in user could use it to list every account, group and role holder in the tenant. Microsoft has retired the module; the setting closes the door for whatever old tooling still knocks on it.

checks.title: People do not read their own BitLocker keys by self-service
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Devices, Device settings.
Set Restrict users from recovering the BitLocker key(s) for their owned devices to Yes.
Make sure the help desk can look up a key and has a way to check who is asking.

userImpact.text: Someone locked out of a laptop asks the help desk for the recovery key and no longer looks it up from another device.

checks.narrative: The recovery key unlocks the disk without the PIN or the person. If the owner can read it from their account, so can anyone who has taken over that account and has the laptop, which is the stolen-laptop case BitLocker exists for.

checks.title: Tenant restrictions block other organisations by default
remediation: In Entra, External Identities, Cross-tenant access settings, Default settings, edit Tenant restrictions defaults.
Under External users and groups choose Block access for all users, and under External applications Block access for all.
Add the organisations your people may sign in to as partner settings, then enforce the policy: through Global Secure Access (NET-017), a Windows policy, or your proxy's header.

userImpact.text: Once enforced, signing in to another organisation's Microsoft 365 from your devices is blocked unless that organisation is allowed.

checks.narrative: Your controls end at the edge of your tenant: a person can sign in to a tenant of their own from a managed laptop and move files into it. Tenant restrictions are how you say which other organisations may be signed in to from your devices. The default that ships allows everything. This check reads the default; the policy still has to be enforced on the device or the network to do anything.

checks.title: App registrations sign in with certificates, not client secrets
remediation: For each application listed, ask its owner how it signs in. A workload in Azure should use a managed identity and needs no credential at all.
Elsewhere, add a certificate to the registration or a federated credential for the platform it runs on, switch the application to it, then delete the secret.
Stop new ones: the tenant app management policy can block new secrets (ID-028).

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people. Each application's owner has a change to make.

checks.narrative: A client secret is a password for an application: a string that works from anywhere, gets pasted into configuration files and pipelines, and is as good as the application's permissions to whoever finds it. A certificate's private key can stay in a vault or on the machine, and a managed identity has no credential to leak. The applications listed still hold a secret.

checks.title: Application certificates are valid for no longer than 180 days
remediation: For each application listed, issue a new certificate valid for 180 days or less and add it to the registration.
Move the application to the new certificate, then remove the old one.
Set the limit in the tenant app management policy so new certificates cannot be longer (ID-029).

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people. Applications need their certificate replaced more often, which is worth automating.

checks.narrative: A certificate that is valid for years is a credential nobody has to think about for years, including after its private key was copied. A short life forces rotation into a routine and bounds how long a stolen key works. The applications listed hold a certificate valid for longer than the limit from start to end.

checks.title: Service principals hold no credentials of their own
remediation: For each application listed, find out who added the credential and why: Entra audit log, activity Add service principal credentials.
If it is in use, put a credential on the app registration instead, switch over, and remove the one on the service principal.
If nobody knows it, remove it and treat it as an incident until explained.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An application's secrets and certificates belong on its registration, where the portal shows them and owners look after them. A credential added to the service principal in your tenant is easy to miss, works just as well, and for an application published by someone else it lets its holder act as that application in your tenant. The signing certificate of a SAML application is not counted.

checks.title: No credential has been added to a Microsoft application
remediation: Treat each application listed as a possible intrusion until explained. Look in the Entra audit log for Add service principal credentials on it: who, when, from where.
Remove the credential, and review what the application's permissions would have let its holder do since it was added.
Limit who can do this: Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator can add credentials to service principals.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: Microsoft's own applications, such as Exchange Online or Microsoft Graph tools, carry broad permissions in every tenant and are never meant to hold a credential of yours. Adding a secret to one of their service principals lets an attacker sign in as that application with those permissions, and it survives a password reset of every account. It is a known way of keeping access after a compromise. There is no routine reason for it.

checks.title: Every AI agent and agent blueprint has an owner
remediation: In Entra, Agent ID, open each agent or blueprint listed and add an owner: the person or team that builds it and runs it.
Give each one two owners where you can, so that one person leaving does not leave it with none.
An agent nobody will own is a candidate for removal: disable it, wait for someone to miss it, then delete it.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An owner is the technical contact for an agent: the one who can change its credentials, see what it is doing and switch it off. An agent with no owner keeps its access, and nobody is placed to notice when it is misused or no longer needed. This check counts the owners on agent identities, on agent blueprints and on the blueprints' service principals. It does not tell an owner whose account is disabled from one who is still here.

checks.title: Every AI agent and agent blueprint has a sponsor
remediation: Open each agent or blueprint listed and add a sponsor: the person in the business who answers for why the agent exists and what it may reach.
A sponsor can be a group, which keeps the role filled when one person moves on.
With Entra ID Governance, a lifecycle workflow can hand an agent's sponsorship to the sponsor's manager when the sponsor leaves.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An owner keeps an agent running; a sponsor answers for it. The sponsor is who is asked whether the agent is still needed, whether its access is still right, and what to do when it misbehaves. Without one, an access review of the agent has nobody to go to and the agent outlives the project it was made for. This check counts sponsors on agent identities, agent blueprints and the blueprints' service principals.

checks.title: No disabled agent is left in the directory
remediation: For each one listed, find out why it was disabled: an incident, a test, or an agent that was retired.
If it is finished with, delete it. Its role assignments, permissions and group memberships go with it.
If it is coming back, leave it with an owner and a date to look again.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: A disabled agent cannot sign in, but it still holds its permissions, its roles and its place in groups, and turning it back on restores all of them at once. Left for months, nobody remembers what it was for or whether the reason it was stopped still stands. This check lists agent identities and blueprints' service principals that are disabled.

checks.title: No agent has lost the blueprint or the agent it belongs to
remediation: An agent identity whose blueprint is not in the tenant has nothing governing how it signs in: delete it, or make it again from a current blueprint.
An agent user whose agent identity is gone is a user account with nothing behind it: remove the account and its licences.
A blueprint's service principal whose blueprint was deleted can be removed once no agent is made from it.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An agent identity is made from a blueprint, and an agent's user account is paired with an agent identity. When the parent is deleted and the child stays, what is left is an identity with access and nothing managing it: no blueprint holding its credentials and settings, or a user account with a mailbox and licences that no agent is behind. A service principal for a blueprint that another organisation publishes is not counted, since its blueprint was never in this tenant.

checks.title: No AI agent holds a privileged directory role
remediation: Remove the role from each agent listed (Entra, Roles and administrators).
Give the agent the narrow permission its task needs instead: one Microsoft Graph permission, or a role scoped to an administrative unit.
Where a privileged change is part of the task, keep that step with a person: the agent prepares it and an administrator carries it out.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An agent acts on what it reads, and what it reads can be written by an attacker: a document, an email, a web page. An agent that holds Global Administrator or another privileged role turns one planted instruction into a change to the tenant. This check looks for a privileged role held by an agent identity, by a blueprint's service principal or by an agent's user account: assigned, eligible, or through a group. A blueprint published by another organisation is named as such.

checks.title: No AI agent holds a high-privilege Microsoft Graph permission
remediation: For each permission listed, ask the agent's owner what it is used for.
Replace it with the narrowest permission that does the job, or with a delegated permission, so the agent can do only what the person using it can.
Remove the grant from the agent or the blueprint. On a blueprint, also take it out of what the blueprint passes on to its agents.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: An application permission on Microsoft Graph works with no person signed in. The ones counted here can change the directory, its policies or who holds a role, or read every mailbox and file. Held by an agent, they are within reach of whatever the agent can be talked into doing. The check reads application permissions granted to agent identities and to blueprints' service principals, whose agents can be given what the blueprint holds. Delegated permissions are not counted.

checks.title: Agent blueprints pass on only the permissions they name
remediation: Open each blueprint listed and look at its inheritable permissions.
Change All allowed to a list of the scopes and roles every agent made from the blueprint needs.
Give a single agent that needs more a grant of its own.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: A blueprint can hand its permissions on an API to every agent made from it. Set to all allowed, each agent gets whatever the blueprint holds on that API, and anything granted to the blueprint later as well. A permission added to the blueprint for one purpose then reaches every agent without anyone deciding that it should.

checks.title: Agent blueprints that expose roles require assignment
remediation: Open each one listed under Enterprise applications, Properties, and set Assignment required to Yes.
Before you do, assign the users, groups and applications that call it, or they lose access.

userImpact.text: A person or application that is not assigned can no longer get a token for the agent and needs to be added.

checks.narrative: A blueprint can define application roles that say what a caller may ask its agents to do. When its service principal does not require assignment, Entra issues a token for it to any user or application in the tenant, and what happens next depends on the agent checking the roles itself. With assignment required, only the callers you chose get a token at all.

checks.title: Agent blueprints have no wildcard or plain-http redirect address
remediation: Open each blueprint listed, Authentication, and replace an address with a wildcard by the exact addresses the agent uses.
Replace http with https. Plain http is fine only for localhost on a developer's machine.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: After a sign-in, Entra sends the result to a redirect address registered on the blueprint. An address with a wildcard matches hosts nobody meant it to, and one over plain http can be read on the way. Either lets someone else receive what was meant for the agent.

checks.title: Agent blueprint credentials are current, few and short-lived
remediation: Remove expired secrets and certificates from each blueprint listed.
Where the agent runs in Azure, or on a platform that can vouch for it, use a managed identity or a federated credential, and delete the secret once that works.
Otherwise keep at most two working secrets, one in use and one for the changeover, each valid for two years or less.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people.

checks.narrative: A blueprint's credential is what lets its agents get tokens. An expired one is clutter that hides the one in use. A long-lived one works for years after it leaks. Several working at once means nobody knows which is in use. A secret kept beside a federated credential is the weaker way in, left open. This check fails a blueprint on any of the four.
